reading.ours: two units of arithmetic per iteration
reading.floor: one unit of arithmetic per iteration
reading.caveat: NOT A PRICE — an instrument check, and it is printed first because nothing below it means anything until it passes. The true ratio is a little UNDER 2: both sides pay the driving loop once, so the exact expectation is (2u + L) / (u + L) with L the loop and u one unit, which at sixteen dependent steps per unit puts it around 1.9. A reading below 1.5 means this process could not resolve a deliberate doubling, and the runner voids the report rather than printing prices under it.

reading.ours: one unit of arithmetic per iteration
reading.floor: the same body again, over its own copy of the same state
reading.caveat: NOT A PRICE — the noise floor. The two sides are identical code over identical, separately-allocated state, so the true ratio is 1.00 exactly and every departure from it printed here was produced by this machine at this moment. The rule that follows is the one the whole table is read under: NO RATIO CLOSER TO 1.00 THAN THIS GAP IS A READING. It also bounds the per-row noise figure, which is the same idea measured again inside every pair — each pair times its floor twice, once before our side and once after, and prints how far the two disagreed.

reading.ours: getValueForSlot on a computed slot over 1 source slot, refreshed against the channel clock — nothing written since
reading.floor: settle it against one reading per source, held in an array beside the source list
reading.caveat: THE QUIET READ, AND ON THE SHIPPED ENGINE IT DOES NOT WALK THE SOURCES AT ALL. `oimRefreshComputedSlot` returns on the slot's `checkedAt` pair matching the channel clock, which is only possible because the clock is ONE scale: nothing was written anywhere, so nothing a derivation reads can have moved. The per-slot arm has no such question to ask and must compare every source reading. At one source that walk is one element, so this row is the narrowest the gap can be. 1024 derivations are settled before the clock starts and read in rotation. RESIDUALS. Both arms derive the same sum over the same entity slots of two fixtures built alike, and the build throws unless every derivation answers the same on both. AGAINST US: our comparison is a CALL to `oimIsRevisionAfter` and walks an EMPTY `sourceComputeds` array first, where the rejected arm compares inline with `!==` — a per-slot counter cannot wrap inside a process and needs no epoch, which is the one structural advantage that design has and it is granted in full. AGAINST THE REJECTED ARM: its readings are an array object per derivation, so every settle chases one more pointer than our two inline fields. OURS IS READ THROUGH ITS OWNER: the 1024 derivations are the held slots of one `OIMComputedCollection` keyed by derivation, and each read is `getValueForSlot`, which pays `assertNotReleased` and a call into `oimRefreshComputedSlot` before the clock compare — charged to us. A derive looks its source list up by the slot's key, which only a write that lands in a source list would reach, and no row here makes one. NO ROW MEASURES BYTES; `src/retained/retainedPairsDerivations.ts` is where that half lives.

reading.ours: a frame of 16 writes; 16 of 256 derivations read once each — deduped at the getter
reading.floor: the same frame — deduped in the channel, by a dependent walk and a frame stamp
reading.caveat: THE SHAPE AN APPLICATION USUALLY HAS, and the one the shipped arm is built for: far more derivations exist than any one frame reads. Ours settles 16 derivations and touches nothing else; the channel arm walks every dependent of all 16 written roots and recomputes each queued derivation whether or not it is read. ABOVE 1.0x HERE WOULD BE THE FINDING [FIGURE STATED IN ADVANCE], because it would mean the per-read source comparison costs more than recomputing derivations nobody wants. Both arms write through the same `OIMEntityCollection` and `OIMChannel`, so the write path is common and cancels; what differs is only where the "already done this frame" question is asked. What no ratio here prices: the getter arm is what makes a derivation nobody reads cost nothing at all, which is a property of the whole engine and not of this frame.

reading.ours: a frame of 16 writes; all 256 derivations read 4 times each — deduped at the getter
reading.floor: the same frame — deduped in the channel, by a dependent walk and a frame stamp
reading.caveat: THE OTHER END, AND THE ONE THAT SHOULD GO AGAINST US: everything derived is wanted, and wanted repeatedly. Ours walks the four sources on the FIRST read of each of the 256 derivations — 1024 comparisons a frame — and answers the other three reads of each from the slot's `checkedAt` pair against the channel clock, through `getValueForSlot` and its `assertNotReleased` every time; the channel arm asks nothing on a read and recomputes only what the writes touched. BELOW 1.0x HERE IS EXPECTED [FIGURE STATED IN ADVANCE]; a row that came out above 1.0x at BOTH ends would mean one arm is not written in its best form and the pair must not be quoted. Read with the row above and never alone: the pair IS the answer, and either row by itself reads as a verdict on "dedup" that neither one supports.

reading.ours: if (!carrier.isPending) { carrier.isPending = true; pending.push(carrier) } — drained as an array
reading.floor: pendingSet.add(carrier) — drained by iterating the Set and clearing it
reading.caveat: ONE OPERATION IS ONE MARK. A frame marks every carrier the stated number of times, in passes over the whole population, and then drains, so a repeat mark is the flag's early return on ours and a hash hit on the Set. The drain runs one counting body per carrier on both arms and both were checked to run the same number before the clock. This is the shape of `OIMChannel.enlist` and its frame loop, hand-written, so one carrier shape reaches each arm; production carriers are megamorphic there, which charges the field reads on our side and not the Set on the other, so the ratio is a lower bound on what the flag costs in the engine.

reading.floor: effectService.createEffect([slot], [], body) with the body comparing `title` against what it saw last
reading.caveat: ONE OPERATION IS ONE ROW WRITE, AND A PASS IS TWO OF THEM PER ROW: every row's `note` moves and a frame runs, then every row's `title` moves and a frame runs. One subscriber per row, mounted before the clock, cares only about `title`. Ours subscribes to the column's own identity, so the `note` frame wakes nobody — the write probes the row's column store and finds no `note` column — and the `title` frame wakes every subscriber; the rejected arm subscribes to the row, so BOTH frames wake every subscriber and its body filters the `note` frame out. Each arm was checked to report exactly one title change per row per pass. The two arms put different slot shapes through the same `update` and the same channel, so the pair is isolated.

reading.ours: effectService.createEffect(rootSlots, [], body) — a new TOIMEffect over 8 roots
reading.floor: createLiteralEffect(channel, rootSlots, body) — a literal over 8 roots, subscribed by a shared function
reading.caveat: THE SHIPPED SERVICE AGAINST THE BENCH'S OWN LITERAL COPY OF ITS ALGORITHM. Ours is the shipped `OIMEffectService`, whose effects are plain `TOIMEffect` objects carrying an `effectService` reference. The floor is a literal copy of the same fields and the same run and dispose steps, kept in this file as module-level functions and a small literal service object (`runEffectIfSourcesChanged`, `setPositionInSubscribedSlot`) because the channel and `OIMSlotOwner.unsubscribeFromSlot` call those through the effect. Both subscribe through the same `OIMSlotOwner.subscribeToSlot`, so `isolate` keeps each arm in its own process. Each arm keeps ONE resident effect alive for the whole process, so the hidden-class loss at a full GC (WHY-EACH-ROW.md, churnChain) is excluded and what remains is the cost of the service call itself. The floor skips the shipped `createEffect`'s source-computed dedup `Set` branch, its try/catch and its frame-scheduling check, none of which does work for an effect with no source computeds. One operation is one effect created and subscribed to 8 roots; the disposal of the pass is in `reset`, untimed.

reading.ours: one write function handed three slot shapes — entity, bucket, column
reading.floor: three write functions, one per slot kind, each handed only its own shape
reading.caveat: ONE OPERATION IS THREE WRITES, one slot of each kind, in the same order on both arms over the same pool of literals. The bodies are byte-identical and are SEPARATE FUNCTION LITERALS — closures minted from one literal share their feedback, so a factory would make the rejected arm polymorphic too and the row would price nothing. These three are the literals `how-many-shapes-reach-the-write-door.test.ts` pins at `OIMChannel.writeWithoutFlushCheck`, so our arm is as polymorphic as production. `isolate` keeps the two arms from sharing a heap history.

reading.ours: one write function handed the three shipped slot shapes
reading.floor: one write function handed three slots minted with one unified shape
reading.caveat: THE HALF OF THE UNIFIED-SHAPE ARGUMENT THAT FAVOURS IT, and it must be read with `alt.slot-shape.three-shapes-against-one-at-the-mint`, which is the half that pays for it. One operation is three writes in the same order over the same pool size on both arms; the only difference is whether the site sees three hidden classes or one. The unified literal carries every field any kind needs, in one order, so it is one map. Above one is the shipped design losing at the write.

reading.ours: updateEntity(slot, patch) on the shipped walk — for…in, own-property-ness proved once
reading.floor: REJECTED: the same write with Object.keys(source) and a walk of that array
reading.caveat: THE SCENARIO THE SOURCE'S OLD FIGURE NAMED, GIVEN A DIRECTORY. The in-place writer's source once put the array-allocating form at 1.099 ms against 479 µs on "ten thousand rows rewritten with the values they already hold" [NO RUN BEHIND THIS FIGURE]. This row is that scenario: ONE OPERATION IS ONE `updateEntity` OF A ROW WITH A PATCH IT ALREADY MATCHES IN ALL SIXTEEN COLUMNS. The population is primed outside the clock so every row holds round zero's values, and the timed patch is round zero's — so every write enumerates sixteen columns, compares sixteen times, moves nothing, and returns having marked nothing. OPERATION COUNT, both arms: 16 `oimIsProtoKey` compares, 16 `oimSameValueZeroGuard` calls, 16 pairs of property loads, and no changed-names array. Ours additionally pays ONE `oimIsPlain` — one `getPrototypeOf` and two reference compares, per write. The floor pays ONE `Object.keys` — a sixteen-element array allocated, filled and abandoned per write. THE DIFFERENCE IS ONE PROTOTYPE PROBE AGAINST ONE SIXTEEN-ELEMENT ARRAY, plus whatever the two enumerations cost each other. THIS IS THE MOST FAVOURABLE SCENARIO THE SHIPPED WALK HAS, and that is why the row beside it exists. Read the two rows together or neither. A FLUSH CLOSES EACH PASS ON BOTH ARMS and is an empty one — nothing was marked. THE WRITE AROUND THE WALK IS IDENTICAL ON BOTH ARMS AND IS INSIDE BOTH NUMBERS: `assertWritable` with the channel's `assertNotFlushing`, `openSubframe`/`closeSubframe`, the writer dispatch, the `length > 0` test, and — on a write that moves something — the changed-names array, `markColumnsChanged`'s column-store probe per moved column, `channel.writeWithoutFlushCheck` and `markContentChanged`. That is a large constant added to the numerator and the denominator alike, so it pulls this ratio toward 1.00 and the printed ratio is a LOWER BOUND on the difference between the two walks. The two nanosecond columns beside it are not pulled anywhere: subtract them to get the per-write difference the row is actually about. THIS PAIR DECLARES `isolate`, AND THE READING IS UNINTERPRETABLE WITHOUT IT. Both arms reach the engine through one compiled function — `OIMEntityCollection.prototype.patchEntity`, whose single call site `this.entityWriter.patchEntity(entitySlot, patch)` would see both writers in one process. Neither would then be inlined, and inlining the column walk into the write is exactly where a walk's advantage lives; worse, the failure is invisible, because a ratio of 1.00 would be equally consistent with "the two walks cost the same" and "each arm ran through caches the other had already made polymorphic". Each side is therefore probed and timed in a process that has never constructed the other, and `build` declines to fill the population it was not asked for — merely FILLING the other design's population teaches V8 its shape, so declining to time it is not enough. What it costs: `noise` now includes process-to-process variation, which is the honest thing for it to include here.
